The Pros and Cons of Refinancing Student Loans
Let's face it, college is expensive. Student loans are becoming a financial hardship for more and more graduates every year. Refinancing at a lower interest rate can potentially allow you to:
Choose between a variable-rate loan and a fixed-rate loan
Release a cosigner from the loan
Make one payment a month instead of several

It is important to note that when you refinance federal student loans through a private lender, you'll no longer be eligible for flexible repayment and forgiveness programs that come with those loans. Through deferment or forbearance, most federal loans will allow you to suspend or reduce your payments under special circumstances, such as unemployment, qualifying active military service or participation in an approved graduate fellowship program. Interest does not continue to accrue during deferment but does continue to accrue during forbearance. Also, federal loans offer Income-Based Repayment (IBR) and Income-Driven Repayment (IDR) plans that base your monthly payments on how much you make or how much you can afford.

If you think you'll need one or more of these features, you might be better off keeping your loans with the government. But if you don't need them, and your priority is saving money, then refinancing could be a great option for you.

A common question asked by student loan borrowers is, "What's the difference between consolidation and refinancing?" The answer depends on the context. As its name suggests, consolidation means combining multiple student loans in to one loan.

Direct Loan Consolidation is a program offered by the government, and it only applies to federal student loans. The interest rate on your new, consolidated loan is a weighted average of your original loans' rates. Therefore, consolidation won't save you money. Moreover, consolidation typically results in the borrower paying more in total interest because consolidated loans are generally stretched out over a longer period.

Student loan refinancing, on the other hand, is when a private lender takes on your loan, or loans, and combines them into one loan at a new rate and repayment schedule. Your new interest rate depends on the market rates, your income and your track record of managing debt.

Along with your income and debt status, your personal credit profile can have a significant impact on which loans are available to you and the rates offered. A high credit rating can save you thousands of dollars over the life of a loan.
Individuals with excellent credit ratings typically have a FICO score above 740
Individuals with good credit ratings typically have a FICO score between 660 and 740
Individuals with fair credit ratings typically have a FICO score between 580 and 660
Individuals with poor credit ratings typically have a FICO score below 580

Your FICO score (an acronym for the credit scoring service, Fair Isaacs Company) is an assigned number between 300 and 850 that indicates to lenders your capacity to repay a loan. It can change regularly, as new information is sent by your creditors to one or more of the three major national credit bureaus, Experian, Trans Union, and Equifax. The higher your FICO score, the more likely you will qualify for a mortgage loan and the best interest rates.
A FICO score is comprised of 5 parts:

Your types of accounts and your payment record; any bankruptcies, legal judgments, wage garnishments, etc.; the severity and amount of late payments; the number of past-due items and when they occurred. (35%)
How much you currently owe and on what types of accounts; number of accounts with balances; the proportion of credit lines still available. (30%)
Time since accounts opened; by specific type of account; since last activity. (15%)
Number of recently opened accounts, by type and date opened; recent credit inquiries and date of inquiries; reestablishment of good credit after payment delinquencies. (10%)
The number and types of credit accounts available for your use. (10%)
By federal law, you're entitled to a free credit report once every 12 months from each of the three major credit bureaus - Experian, TransUnion, or Equifax.
